card.hook: Ever seen a building that looks like it was drawn with a ruler and then dipped in icing? That's Budapest's Parliament, and from across the river it's almost perfectly symmetrical.
card.stand_here: Stand at Batthyány tér, on the Buda bank by the riverside embankment next to the square. Face the Parliament's river facade across the Danube, and you'll get a straight-on view.
card.zoom: Start at 1x and see how much of the facade fits. Go to 2x or more (depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the dome and towers. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of embankment and sky around it.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the dome on the central vertical line and keep the phone level, so the long roofline doesn't slope.
card.best_time: Around sunset and just after, when the building's lights come on. The lit facade can reflect in the water, so wait for a gap in the boat traffic and take a few shots.
card.selfie_here: Try Kossuth Lajos tér, on the square in front of the main entrance, with the Parliament behind you. Use the front camera and step to the side of the square, because the middle of it hides most of the dome. One traveller's tip is the stone steps behind the building, where the dome fills the background.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the Batthyány tér embankment to stand a few steps back and face the river, while you stand on the embankment with the Parliament across the water behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Going inside the Parliament needs a guided tour, and photography is restricted in parts of the interior, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the two halves of the building so even that your friends ask if you cheated with a mirror.
card.good_to_know: Imre Steindl designed the Parliament and it opened in 1902. It's about 268 m long and 96 m high, still the largest building in Hungary, and the height nods to the 1896 millennium celebrations. It carries 242 sculptures inside and out, many of them rulers and military figures.

card.hook: Imagine a huge butter-yellow building sitting in a park, with a castle looking at it from across the road. That's Széchenyi Thermal Bath, and it's very easy to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand at Széchenyi Gyógyfürdő, on the street side of the main front. The phone icon on the map is right at the building, so there's no extra walk. Face the building, square to the middle, with the park and Vajdahunyad Castle behind you across the road.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x, because the building is wide and you'll want the whole yellow front in. If you can step back, try 1x for a more natural look. If your phone has zoom 2x to 5x, use it for details on the central part of the façade.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and keep your phone upright and level so the walls don't lean, then tap the yellow wall and slide it a touch darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the sun lights up the front of the building. The bath isn't lit up at night, so evening shots will be dark.
card.selfie_here: Try the lawn or gardens in front of the main façade, on the castle side. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the yellow building fill the background over your shoulder (treat this spot as approximate). If you have a bath ticket, the steps of the outdoor pools are a popular selfie spot, with the yellow walls framing you from behind.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the road on the Vajdahunyad Castle side, so the whole façade fits, while you stand in front of the main entrance.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos for personal use are fine, but respect other guests' privacy. Photographing other bathers is frowned upon and staff may stop you, so keep inside shots on the architecture. Drones are not allowed over the complex.

card.hook: Picture a long, pale palace sitting on top of a hill, with a chain-hung bridge leading your eye straight to it. That's the postcard shot of Buda Castle, and it looks good even on a small phone screen.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Pest embankment just south of Széchenyi István tér and face the river. The castle is about 700 m away in a straight line to the south-west, across the Chain Bridge, so you want the whole bridge span lined up in front of it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which fits the bridge and the castle together. Try zoom 0.5x only if you're close to the bridge and want its full length. If the castle looks small, zoom 2x gets you a tighter shot of the hill.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the castle, then drag the slider to make the picture a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out and the lit buildings keep their colour.
card.best_time: Go at sunset or after dark, when the castle is lit. At night, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the railing or a wall to keep the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Head up into the castle grounds to the Matthias Fountain, a local photo favourite with heroic statues. Use the front camera (zoom 0.5x if your phone has it) and stand with the castle façade over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Pest side of the Chain Bridge, where the castle is framed across the river, while you stand a little way in front of them with the castle behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The Chain Bridge can be slippery in wet weather, so watch your step. Big river cruise ships can moor along the embankment and block the view, so check the dock before you settle on a spot. The castle's museums may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the whole Chain Bridge and the castle roofline in one frame, with the bridge deck dead level. No wonky bridge allowed!
card.good_to_know: The first castle here was completed in 1265. The Baroque palace you see today was built between 1749 and 1769, badly damaged in the Second World War, and rebuilt in a simpler Baroque style. It now houses the Hungarian National Gallery, the Budapest Historical Museum and the National Széchényi Library.

card.hook: Most people photograph the basilica from the square, but the sneaky-good shot is from a side street. Zrínyi utca squeezes the facade between two rows of buildings, like a picture frame someone built for you.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which is wide enough to fit the whole facade between the buildings. Switch to 0.5x only if you're close or want more sky, and try 2x or 5x to pick out the dome or the towers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the centre of the doorway up with the middle vertical line, so the buildings on each side balance and the dome sits neatly above.
card.best_time: After dark the facade is floodlit, so it's a lovely time for night mode, but lighting times can change, so check current hours locally. In December the square has a Christmas market, which changes what's in your foreground.
card.selfie_here: Head to Szent István tér, the wide paved square in front of the facade. Stand with the church at your back, use the front camera, and try 0.5x to squeeze in the fountain and café terraces too.
card.ask_someone: Stand at a corner of the big square and ask a passer-by to frame you with the whole church behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash isn't permitted inside the church, and photos aren't appropriate during Mass or other services.
card.challenge: Can you get the doorway exactly on the centre gridline with both side buildings looking like twins? Bonus points if a stranger walks through the middle of the shot.
card.good_to_know: Guides often call the view from Zrínyi utca the most photographed view of the basilica. For a different picture, the Citadella shows the dome far away among the bridges, Elisabeth Bridge and the Pest rooftops. Climbing the dome gives you city views rather than photos of the church itself, so you don't need it for this shot.

card.hook: Picture a wedding-cake castle that someone forgot to put a bride on, and you've got Fisherman's Bastion. All white stone, pointy cone roofs and arches that repeat like a catchy chorus.
card.stand_here: Stand in the courtyard in front of Matthias Church, beside the Bastion, near the statue of King Stephen I. Face the statue with the church rising behind it, and the Bastion's towers will sit to the north as your backdrop.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the statue with the church and towers behind it. Drop to 0.5x for the arches and stairs, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for tower roofs and far-off details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the towers standing straight, and put the statue on one third of the frame.
card.best_time: Get there before about 9 a.m., when the terraces are quietest and you won't have a crowd photobombing every shot. Early arrivals usually get much emptier terraces.
card.selfie_here: Climb either of the two front side staircases and turn so the turrets are directly behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x to squeeze in as many pointy roofs as you can, and try to arrive before about 9 to 10 am, because this is one of the most popular framings.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the left staircase while you walk down the steps with the Bastion behind you; it's a classic shot, and it's at its best at sunrise.
card.rules_and_safety: The lower terrace is free, but the upper terrace and towers are ticketed during the day, so check the official site for current tickets and hours. It gets busy, so keep an eye on your bag and phone, as pickpockets target tourists here.
card.challenge: Can you get all seven towers into one photo without anyone's elbow in it? Bonus points if you manage it with a straight face.
card.good_to_know: The Bastion's seven towers stand for the seven chieftains who founded Hungary in 895. Architect Frigyes Schulek built it between 1895 and 1902 on the base of an older stretch of castle wall. The name probably comes from the guild of fishermen linked to this part of the wall, and the whole Buda Castle District has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the courtyard in front of Matthias Church, beside the Bastion, near the statue of King Stephen I. Face the statue with the church rising behind it, and the Bastion's towers will sit to the north as your backdrop.

card.hook: Walk in and the first thing you'll want is the long view down the hall, with the iron roof running away over a sea of colourful stalls. Then you'll smell the paprika and forget about the photo for a minute.
card.stand_here: Head for the Great Market Hall at Fővám square, where the phone icon on the map sits right at the hall itself. Face down the main aisle so the steel roof runs straight away from you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze in the whole hall and roof. Switch to 1x for stalls, then try 2x or 5x for details like strings of paprika (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the main aisle up so the roof's steel framework runs straight toward the far end, and keep your phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the stalls are freshly laid out and there's usually more room in the aisles. For the outside of the building, pick a bright, dry day so the colourful Zsolnay roof tiles really glow.
card.selfie_here: Stand out on Fővám square in front of the main neo-Gothic façade, with the entrance and tiled roof behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and hold your arm a little high so the roof fits over your shoulder. Expect other snapshot-takers to be there too.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Fővám square across from the hall, while you stand in front of the entrance, so the full front and tiled roof fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask before photographing stallholders or their faces. It's a working market, so check the official site for current opening times and any photography rules before you go.
card.challenge: Find the reddest paprika display in the hall and fill the whole frame with it, so your friends can almost smell the picture.
card.good_to_know: The Great Market Hall is the largest and oldest indoor market in Budapest. It opened on 15 February 1897 and was designed by Samu Pecz. It was badly damaged in World War II, then restored and reopened in 1997.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the Great Market Hall at Fővám square, where the phone icon on the map sits right at the hall itself. Face down the main aisle so the steel roof runs straight away from you.

card.hook: Two stone towers, a sweep of iron chains and a castle sitting on the hill behind them: this is the Budapest postcard, and you can get it in one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand in Széchenyi István tér on the Pest embankment, just south of the bridgehead, next to the Gresham Palace. The middle of the bridge is to the west, about 4 minutes on foot from there, so face west with Buda Castle rising behind the span.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x with your phone held sideways, which should fit the whole span with the castle behind it. If a tower or the far end gets cut off, step back or tap zoom 0.5x. For a tighter shot that makes the castle look closer to the bridge, try zoom 2x or higher, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the bridge deck up with a horizontal line so everything sits nice and level.
card.best_time: Come for blue hour, about 15 to 20 minutes after sunset, when the bridge lights are on and the sky still has some colour. Peek at the river before you go, because moored cruise ships can block the view from Pest.
card.selfie_here: Try the pedestrian island at Széchenyi István tér on the Pest side, with the bridge gates and Buda Castle centred behind you. One guide picks it as the best selfie spot, so check it on the map. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and try 0.5x so the bridge fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo from Eötvös Square, near the Four Seasons Hotel Gresham Palace, where the whole bridge fits end to end with Castle Hill behind it.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge is closed to private cars, so the deck is calm for walking. If you plan to visit Halászbástya, check the official site first, as the towers there are ticketed.
card.challenge: Walk across and find the stone lions, then snap one with the chains curving away behind it. Bonus points if the lion looks more photogenic than you.
card.good_to_know: The bridge opened in 1849 as the first permanent bridge across the Danube in Hungary, and its 202-metre main span was among the longest in the world at the time. It was blown up in January 1945, rebuilt and reopened in 1949, then reopened again in August 2023 after a long renovation. The stone lions were carved by János Marschalkó and installed in 1852.

card.hook: Some of the iron shoes sit neatly side by side. Others are tipped over, as if someone has only just stepped out of them. This is a memorial, so it's a place for a quiet, careful photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on the walkway at the shoes on the Pest bank of the Danube promenade, about 300 metres south of the Hungarian Parliament. Crouch low and face along the row toward the Parliament.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole row with the river behind it. Switch to 1x for a calmer, more natural view, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out one pair without leaning over the shoes.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the nearest shoe, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky stays blue and the iron keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go in the late afternoon or early morning. The light is low and the shadows along the row are long.
card.selfie_here: Skip the selfie at this one. Save your photos of yourself for another spot, with the front camera, zoom 0.5x and a landmark over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Please don't step among the shoes, sit on them or pose in front of them. Treat it like a grave, wait for people to move away, and take your picture quietly from the side of the walkway.
card.challenge: Find the one pair that stops you, maybe a child's shoes, and let the river blur softly behind it.
card.good_to_know: There are sixty pairs of iron shoes. They remember people who were made to take off their shoes and were shot at the water's edge in the winter of 1944-45. The memorial was unveiled on 16 April 2005, created by film director Can Togay with sculptor Gyula Pauer. Cast-iron signs in Hungarian, English and Hebrew explain it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the walkway at the shoes on the Pest bank of the Danube promenade, about 300 metres south of the Hungarian Parliament. Crouch low and face along the row toward the Parliament.

card.hook: Here's a building that looks like it's been iced by a pastry chef, and it's sitting right at the Pest end of the Chain Bridge. Gresham Palace has a long, decorated front and an open square to back up into, so you can fit nearly all of it in.
card.stand_here: Walk to the small grassy patch in front of the facade on Széchenyi István tér, with the hotel entrance behind it. Face east, straight ahead, and the whole front of the palace is in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole front, straight on. If it won't all fit from the grass, drop to 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the decoration on the upper floors.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line them up with the building's vertical edges, because a straight-on facade shows every tilt.
card.best_time: Pick a time when the sky is fairly clear and the light is soft, so the stonework and decoration show up well. For evening shots, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body.
card.selfie_here: Step into the Gresham Palace entrance hall and stand on the decorative tiled floor, with the Art Nouveau interior behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and tilt the phone down a little so the floor and the mosaics both sneak into the frame.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo while you stand on the grass patch in front of the facade, and ask them to step back so the whole palace fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The palace is a hotel, so its rooms and balconies are private. Take your photos from outside, and shoot inside only in the public areas. Personal photos there are fine, but professional shoots may need hotel approval.
card.challenge: Get the facade perfectly straight with the entrance dead centre, and no leaning walls. Tap the screen on the building and check it against the gridlines before you click.
card.good_to_know: Gresham Palace was built between 1904 and 1906 as the foreign headquarters of the London-based Gresham Life Assurance Company, and it opened in 1907. It's named after Sir Thomas Gresham, a 16th-century English financier. The architects were Zsigmond Quittner and Jozsef Vago, and after decades of decline it was rebuilt and reopened as a luxury hotel in 2004.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the small grassy patch in front of the facade on Széchenyi István tér, with the hotel entrance behind it. Face east, straight ahead, and the whole front of the palace is in front of you.

card.hook: Most buildings make you hunt for a good angle. The Opera House hands you one: it's symmetrical, so if you stand square-on, the whole front lines up like it's posing for you.
card.stand_here: Cross Andrássy út and stand on the far pavement, straight opposite the main entrance, about 85 m from the Opera House. It's to the north-west of you, so face it square-on.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x. If the whole front won't fit, step back a bit or try zoom 0.5x, but keep the building away from the edges because it can look stretched there. For a second shot, walk along the tree-lined avenue and zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) so the trees lead your eye to the building.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the main entrance on the middle line and keep the phone level so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Dusk or evening, when the façade is lit, is the best bet. Early morning is another option if you'd like softer light.
card.selfie_here: Go to the far side of Andrássy Avenue, next to the small park islands, and turn your back on the Opera House. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) and hold it a little low so the façade fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the far pavement by the small park islands and frame the full width of the building, while you stand in front of the entrance.
card.rules_and_safety: Photographing the outside needs no ticket. Inside, photos are allowed on guided tours, but flash is restricted. Photos and videos are strictly prohibited during an evening performance. Use the pedestrian crossings and keep clear of the traffic when you step back to frame your shot.
card.challenge: Zoom in and see if you can get both composer statues, Erkel and Liszt, in one shot with the entrance between them.
card.good_to_know: Miklós Ybl designed the Opera House in a neo-Renaissance style with Baroque touches. Building began in 1875 and it opened on 27 September 1884. The statues of the composers Ferenc Erkel and Franz Liszt, by Alajos Stróbl, stand in niches either side of the main entrance. After a long restoration it reopened on 12 March 2022.

card.hook: Picture an angel perched on a column about 36 m high, holding a crown, with two curved colonnades of bronze rulers spread out on either side. Heroes' Square is built to fit in one wide, tidy phone photo.
card.stand_here: Stand in Hősök tere, at the back of the square near the Millennium Monument. The middle of the square lies to the south-west of this point, so face that way to take in the colonnades and the column.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze in the whole colonnade and column, then try 1x for a calmer, more symmetrical shot. Zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) gets you close to the statues or the angel on top.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the column on the centre line and hold your phone level so the colonnades balance and the columns don't lean.
card.best_time: Sunrise gives you the emptiest square, and tour groups tend to show up later in the day. Blue hour is lovely too, when the statues are floodlit, so switch on night mode and tuck your elbows in to keep things sharp.
card.selfie_here: Try the back of the square near the Millennium Monument, by the column with Archangel Gabriel. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it low so the colonnades and the column fit behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Traffic circles the square, so use the marked crossings and keep an eye out for cars if you step toward the edges.
card.challenge: Zoom in to 5x (if your phone has it) and take a close-up of the angel's crown, then show it off next to your wide shot.
card.good_to_know: Building began in 1896 for the thousandth anniversary of the Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin and was mostly done by 1900. The monument was inaugurated in 1905, and the angel stands 4.8 m high. The square has been officially called Heroes' Square since 1932.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Hősök tere, at the back of the square near the Millennium Monument. The middle of the square lies to the south-west of this point, so face that way to take in the colonnades and the column.

card.stand_here: Head to Szent Gellért tér, the square directly opposite the bath entrance, and stand facing the entrance. The Liberty Bridge pylons should show up beside the building.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the whole facade and a bridge pylon into one frame. Switch to 1x for a natural look, then 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the entrance and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the front of the building up with them, and keep your phone level so the verticals stay straight instead of leaning.

card.selfie_here: Stand on Gellért Square in front of the grand entrance, with the statue-decorated facade behind you. Use your front camera, hold it a little low and, if your phone offers a wider front option, try it so the building fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the Buda-side end of Liberty Bridge, while you stand in front of the grand entrance so they can frame you with the facade behind.
card.rules_and_safety: The bath is closed for a major renovation until about 2028, so only the outside can be photographed. Check the current status before you travel.
card.challenge: Get the whole facade and one Liberty Bridge pylon in the same shot with perfectly straight lines. Gridlines are your friend.
card.good_to_know: The Gellért Thermal Bath is an Art Nouveau building on the Buda bank of the Danube, with Gellért Hill behind it and the Liberty Bridge beside it. A Hungarian heritage guide describes Szent Gellért tér as one of the finest squares in Buda. card.hook: The stripes get you first: yellow and red brick, a big round rose window, and two onion-domed towers that look like they belong in a storybook. The catch is that the square out front is small, so you'll need to find some distance.
card.stand_here: Stand on Dohány utca, on the opposite (west) side of Dohány Street, across from the main facade. Face the synagogue so both towers rise in front of you from base to dome.
card.zoom: If you're close to the kerb, try zoom 0.5x so both towers and the domes fit. If you can step back, zoom 1x looks more natural, with less stretching at the edges.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the middle of the facade up with the centre grid line, so the two towers sit evenly, and keep the phone level so they don't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and there are fewer people in the street. The red and yellow stripes look their best then.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at 0.5x from the pavement and tilt your arm so the towers rise over your shoulder. Keep it quick and quiet, and save the courtyard for remembering rather than posing.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by and ask them to stand on the far pavement across Dohány Street, so the full height of both towers fits in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: No photos are taken during Shabbat services, and flash and selfie sticks are banned in the museum. Personal photos are allowed inside, but recording the guide is not. The courtyard holds graves from the winter of 1944-45, so treat it as a place of remembrance, not a backdrop for posed portraits.
card.challenge: Can you fit the rose window and both onion domes in one straight, level shot, with no leaning towers?
card.good_to_know: This is the largest synagogue in Europe. Ludwig Förster designed it, it was built between 1854 and 1859, and it originally seated nearly 3,000 people. The towers reach about 43 metres, and Dohány Street was the border of the Budapest Ghetto during the Holocaust.

card.hook: Here's a fun one: this castle started life in 1896 as wood and cardboard, and now it's brick, stone and very good at posing. Towers, rooftops and a lake that doubles the view.
card.stand_here: Head for the lakeside path in Városliget, near the ice rink. The castle is about 344 m to the north-east, so face it across the water and fit the whole facade in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the full facade and its reflection. Go to 0.5x to take in more water and sky, then zoom 2x for towers and carved details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the waterline across the middle, so the towers and their reflection get equal space.
card.best_time: Go before 9 a.m. on a calm morning, when the lake is still and the paths are nearly empty. In winter, the ice rink and event setups can block the best angles from the bridge.
card.selfie_here: Stand near the centre of the small footbridge that leads from the park into the castle grounds, with the castle behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tilt up so the towers sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the far side of the lake looking west, while you stand in front of the castle towers on the near side, so the towers and reflection fill the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos in the open courtyard are free. Inside the museum you may need a separate photo ticket and flash is generally not allowed, so check the official site before you go. A planned photoshoot, such as a wedding, needs a special permit.
card.challenge: Find the spot where the water is so still that you can't tell which tower is the real one, then ask a friend to guess.
card.good_to_know: Ignác Alpár designed the castle for the 1896 Millennial Exhibition. It was rebuilt in brick and stone between 1904 and 1908. It mixes Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque parts, and it also houses the Museum of Hungarian Agriculture.

card.hook: You've climbed a steep hill in comfortable shoes, and the reward is a river with bridges lined up like they're posing for you. From up here, the Chain Bridge, Elisabeth Bridge and the Parliament all fit in one view.
card.stand_here: Head to the terrace below the Liberty Statue (Szabadság-szobor), on the Citadella side of the summit. Face across the Danube and you'll have the Pest skyline right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole river view. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the Parliament or the Chain Bridge. Use 0.5x only if you want the statue or the sweep of the terrace in the shot.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the river on the lower line, keep the horizon level, and tap the Parliament, then slide it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go for golden hour before sunset, then stick around for blue hour. After sunset, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the railing or a wall to keep things sharp.
card.selfie_here: Try the Pest-side end of Liberty Bridge beside Fővám tér, next to the Central Market Hall, or stroll the Danube promenade on the Pest bank. Both are described as good places to see Gellért Hill and the Citadella, so use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) with the green hill over your shoulder. We haven't confirmed the exact selfie spot on the ground, so have a look around when you get there.
card.ask_someone: At the Pest end of Liberty Bridge near the Central Market Hall, ask a passer-by to stand there and shoot you with the bridge and Gellért Hill behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The hill can be slippery in winter, so take care when taking photos. The Citadella has had long renovation work and some areas may be closed, so check the official site before you go, and expect a few barriers in the background of wide shots.
card.challenge: Get the Chain Bridge, Elisabeth Bridge and the Parliament all in one frame, with the bridges leading your eye to the Parliament like arrows.
card.good_to_know: Gellért Hill is 235 m high, and the Citadella at the top stands about 140 m above the river. The Habsburgs built the Citadella after the 1848-49 uprising, and the Soviet Red Army put up the Liberty Statue beside it to mark its Second World War victory. Since 1987 the hill has been part of the UNESCO World Heritage site 'the Banks of the Danube'.

card.hook: Picture a long green strip floating in the middle of the Danube, with no traffic noise and a path that changes view at every bend. That's Margaret Island, and it's less a single landmark than a whole scene to wander through.
card.stand_here: On Margaret Island, stand about 500 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Once you're on the island, pick a path with trees and water on either side of you for a framed view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole island and river in. Go to 1x for paths and lawns, then 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for details like the Water Tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn the gridlines on and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line so your wide shots look nice and level.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives you softer light and fewer people on the paths. In summer the Music Fountain has music and light shows, so an evening visit could suit it. Check the official site for times.
card.selfie_here: Head up the path to the Budapest sign and stand in the middle of the lettering, or you'll blend into it. If the sign is still there, that's your 'I was here' shot. For a second option, climb the slightly raised grass slope on the north side of the Music Fountain and turn so the fountain and Margaret Bridge sit behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x if your phone offers it, and keep the landmark over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed across the island, including at the fountain shows. At the northern tip the shoreline is only centimeters from the water, so take care there. Some venues, like the water park, the Water Tower exhibition and the open-air theatre, may be ticketed or have set hours.
card.challenge: Take one photo at every bend in the path, then pick the one where the island looks most like your own private park.
card.good_to_know: The island is named after Saint Margaret, daughter of King Béla IV, who lived in the Dominican convent here. The ruins of medieval churches and convents are a reminder that it was a religious centre in the Middle Ages. It became a public garden in 1908, and the octagonal Art Nouveau Water Tower dates from 1911.

card.hook: Picture a church wearing a patterned tile roof like a fancy knitted jumper, with white fairy-tale towers standing right next to it. That's Matthias Church, and the Bastion is the best seat in the house.
card.stand_here: Stand on the lower/central terrace of Halászbástya (the Fisherman's Bastion), among the white towers, and face the church. From here it lies to the south-west.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the Bastion's arches, the roof and the spires all in one shot. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, more natural look. Then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the tile pattern and the spires.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tiled roof, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the bright sky doesn't wash out those colours.
card.best_time: Sunrise is your best bet: the square is quiet and the light is warm. Late afternoon can look lovely on the roof too. Mid-morning and summer are the busiest times, so expect people in your shots then.
card.selfie_here: Find the statue of King Stephen I on the terrace beside the Bastion, with Matthias Church rising behind it. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze more church in, and keep the roof over your shoulder. Check which way the church sits when you arrive, so you know where to turn.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the upper level of the Bastion (the ticketed part) and turn toward the church, while you walk in the courtyard below with Matthias Church behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The lower terrace of the Bastion is free, but the upper level needs a ticket. The church is a place of worship and closes to visitors during services, so check the official sites before you go.
card.challenge: Take the same spires twice, once through a Bastion arch and once without, then pick your winner.
card.good_to_know: The church you see today is late Gothic, from the second half of the 14th century, and it was heavily restored in the late 19th century. The last two Kings of Hungary, Franz Joseph I and Charles IV, were crowned here. King Matthias rebuilt the southern tower in 1470, and since the 19th century the church has carried his name.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the lower/central terrace of Halászbástya (the Fisherman's Bastion), among the white towers, and face the church. From here it lies to the south-west.

card.hook: Yes, Váci utca is busy and very touristy. But that long, car-free corridor of façades is also one of the easiest streets in Budapest to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand in Vörösmarty tér, at the northern end of Váci utca next to the Gerbeaud café. The subject is about 315 m to the south-east, so face south and look straight down the street.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole street and the square in one frame. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pull the far end of the street closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the point where the street disappears near the centre, and keep the café and the Vörösmarty statue low in the frame.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is lovely, because the low sun throws long shadows between the buildings. For a quieter street, go on a weekday before 9 AM.
card.selfie_here: Try Vörösmarty tér in the Christmas fair area, where a Budapest selfie guide suggests putting Váci Street's buildings behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and let the street fill the background over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo while you stand at the northern end of Váci utca where it meets the square, with the Gerbeaud café in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: If a stranger invites you into a bar, politely decline, because the street is known for scams like that. It's also busy, so keep an eye on your phone and belongings while you line up your shot.
card.challenge: Take the same street three times, at 0.5x, 1x and 2x, and see which one feels most like you were really there.
card.good_to_know: Váci utca is named after the city of Vác and is one of central Budapest's main pedestrian streets. Further along you'll find a mural of Saint George slaying a dragon and the Serbian Orthodox church of Saint George, both good extra shots. In winter a Christmas market on the square can block the view and add crowds.

card.hook: A 14 m bronze figure holds a palm leaf over Budapest, and she's surprisingly hard to squeeze into one phone screen. Good news: the whole city is waiting behind her, so you've got plenty to play with.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the Szabadság-szobor, on the statue terrace on the Gellért Hill summit, where the phone icon on the map sits. Face the Pest side, so the statue is in front of you with the Danube, Parliament and the skyline behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the tall statue and the city fit together, stepping back along the terrace and tilting the phone up. Then try 1x for a cleaner view, and 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out Parliament across the river.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the statue on one vertical line and let the river and skyline fill the other side, keeping the horizon level.
card.best_time: Golden hour and blue hour are the sweet spots, when the city lights come on. One guide suggests arriving 30 to 45 minutes before sunset.
card.selfie_here: Head for the terrace below the Liberty Statue, or the open platform out front at the Citadella end of the summit. Face down toward the city with the statue at your back, use the front camera, and try 0.5x to get the statue over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a different shot, stand on the Buda end of Liberty Bridge near Szent Gellért tér, where the hilltop statue is visible above you, and ask a passer-by to photograph you with it overhead.
card.rules_and_safety: Gellért Hill and the statue are free to visit, but the Citadella area has been under renovation and some parts may have limited access, so check the official site before you go. One guide warns that the hill can be quite slippery in winter, so take care when taking photos.
card.challenge: Can you line the statue up on a gridline with Parliament peeking out across the river? Bonus points if the palm leaf stays in the frame.
card.good_to_know: The statue was first put up in 1947 and designed by Zsigmond Kisfaludi Strobl. The 14 m bronze figure stands on a 26 m pedestal, so it rises well above the hilltop. Its inscription was changed after 1989, and it now remembers those who gave their lives for Hungary's independence, freedom and prosperity.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the Szabadság-szobor, on the statue terrace on the Gellért Hill summit, where the phone icon on the map sits. Face the Pest side, so the statue is in front of you with the Danube, Parliament and the skyline behind it.

card.hook: Picture a bright green bridge, a tram sliding across it and a big hill sitting right behind. Liberty Bridge practically poses for you, and it's one of the easiest bridges in Budapest to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand in Fővám tér, beside the Great Market Hall at the Pest end of the bridge. From there the middle of the bridge is to the west, about 3 minutes on foot, so face west and you'll see the green span rising toward Gellért Hill.
card.zoom: Start at 1x. The bridge is only about 334 metres long, so the whole span fits in one frame. Then try zoom 2x or more (depends on your phone) for a Turul bird on a mast or a tram crossing, or 0.5x if you want the market hall and the square in the shot too.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the bridge up along one so the span looks level and the masts stand upright.
card.best_time: Go at sunset and arrive about an hour early. You can try angles while the warm light hits the green steel, then stay for the city lights coming on behind the bridge. After dark, switch on night mode and hold your phone as still as you can.
card.selfie_here: Take it in Fővám tér at the Pest end, with the green ironwork and the Turul bird pillars behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze more bridge in, and tilt the phone so the bridge sits over your shoulder. Check on site that the angle works.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in Szent Gellért tér on the Buda bank, with the bridge stretching across the frame, while you stand in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the walkways and don't climb the ironwork. The framework is steep and the steel gets hot in the afternoon.
card.challenge: Wait for a tram to roll onto the bridge and snap it with Gellért Hill behind. Bonus points if you spot a Turul too.
card.good_to_know: Liberty Bridge was built between 1894 and 1896 as part of the Millennium celebrations. It was first named after Emperor Franz Joseph, who inserted the last silver rivet himself. The Turul is a falcon-like bird from Hungarian legend, and big bronze ones sit on top of the four masts.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Fővám tér, beside the Great Market Hall at the Pest end of the bridge. From there the middle of the bridge is to the west, about 3 minutes on foot, so face west and you'll see the green span rising toward Gellért Hill.
